report:
# Bounded response batching — 2026-09-05

Batching ordinary handler responses raised the same binary's pipeline-16 median
from **233,768 to 1,220,510 responses/s (5.22×)**. A separate one-core comparison
measured **1,833,059 for Zig versus 2,617,684 for libreactor**. Assertions remain
enabled, callbacks still run for every request, and all output cells are reserved
at startup. This closes much of the original gap; it does not establish parity,
production capacity or reliable request tails.

## Exact sources and experiments

Measured commit **b7ac35558dea3e418e7dab5e41b1d3bb9054ca73**, exact Zig 0.16.0
ReleaseSafe. Linux binary SHA-256:
`be403bbe9f756b7e07aa3e87b489471b0f888a695a00e625115f7dccf096ec46`.
The subsequent **5620905193e496af1c4b297a576c4fe7edd6c4a9** adds a cancellation
observation counter/test and documentation; the benchmark does not silently
identify that later binary as its measured input.

Host omarx1: Intel Core Ultra 7 258V, x86_64 Omarchy 4.0.2, kernel
7.1.9-arch1-2, glibc 2.44, GCC 16.2.1 20260810, io_uring_disabled=0.
Pinned contenders, compiler/container differences, wrk hashes and known latency
defect are in [the initial comparison](2026-09-05-comparison.md).
No build overlapped a timed workload on Linux.

Both sweeps used IPv4 loopback, 128 connections, pipeline 1/16, four wrk threads
on CPUs 3–7, three shuffled repetitions, seed 20260905, one-second warmup and
five-second measurement. Each trial separately checked 32 exact bodies, framing,
Server and advancing Date before load. Timed wrk validates parsing/status/error
counts, not every body byte. mrhttp preserves its lowercase `Hello, world!`;
Zig/libreactor use `Hello, World!`. Different headers and callback/resource
policies remain disclosed.

The [24-trial sweep](2026-09-05-batch/results.json) ran 17:30:32–17:33:34 UTC.
Servers could use CPUs 0–2. Zig has one I/O/handler thread, whereas each contender
uses three serving processes plus a parent. Equal allowed CPU sets are not equal
actual parallelism. Median responses/s (min–max):

| Configuration | Pipeline 1 | Pipeline 16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Zig batch 1 | 198,087 (198,000–198,926) | 233,768 (229,994–239,762) |
| Zig batch 16 | 195,144 (190,493–214,983) | 1,220,510 (1,149,870–1,376,905) |
| mrhttp | 416,040 (374,243–628,336) | 3,593,634 (3,493,275–3,666,470) |
| libreactor | 413,962 (405,017–419,191) | 4,630,824 (4,353,429–4,891,632) |

All 24 trials/warmups passed: 165,195,315 timed responses, 768 exact preflights,
zero reported transport/status errors. Pipeline batch-16 runs used exactly one
gather operation per 16 completed responses in these whole-session counters,
with zero suffix compaction bytes; batch-1 runs copied roughly 533–546 MB.
Heap peaks were 29,618,624 bytes for batch16 versus 20,648,384 for batch1.
All owned connection/operation counts drained to zero, no late framework
allocation occurred, and every observed batch/callback/connection count stayed
within its configured limit. Counters cover preflight, warmup and timed phases.

The [one-core sweep](2026-09-05-batch/single-core.json) ran 17:35:17–17:36:45 UTC.
Both servers were restricted to CPU0. Libreactor's existing affinity-based launch
created one serving child plus an idle parent; Zig retained its single owner.
No process/thread-count normalization or inferred scaling is used:

| Configuration | Pipeline 1 | Pipeline 16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Zig batch16 | 196,870 (192,624–200,073) | 1,833,059 (1,829,283–1,875,441) |
| libreactor | 222,052 (205,497–224,319) | 2,617,684 (2,614,945–2,631,774) |

All 12 trials/warmups passed: 73,490,913 timed responses and 384 exact preflights.
The pipeline gap is approximately 1.43× in this setup. Approximate server CPU
was 83% for Zig and 64% for libreactor, calculated over the outer process
measurement interval; it is not a precise cycles/request profile. The changed
CPU mask coincides with a higher Zig rate, but these separate short sweeps do
not isolate migration/cache, frequency or desktop variation as the cause.
Affinity does not reserve CPUs, and client/thermal limits remain. Retain raw wrk
histograms but reject corrected percentiles as trustworthy tail measurements.

The earlier 344k gather checkpoint is preserved independently. This patch also
changes the scheduler and retained metadata; its batch1 diagnostic is a slower
233k in this later sweep. Do not substitute either older number for the
same-binary batch1/batch16 comparison, or claim every changed path improved.

## Architecture and ownership

Default inline/zero-worker execution and gathered header/body output remain.
Config.response_batch_limit is 1–16, default16; worker mode reserves one cell.
Each inline connection owns startup output/header/chunk cells. The common
request/writer callback freezes a finished cell, advances the input cursor and
can handle the next already-buffered request without waiting for a send. Input
bytes remain immutable while any response borrows them. This supports generated
output and distinct borrowed request bodies, without a plaintext cache.

At most 80 framing/payload spans feed stable startup iovecs/msghdr storage;
Linux submits SENDMSG through io_uring and macOS uses nonblocking sendmsg/kqueue.
Aggregate send_chunk/i32 limits and cross-span partial completion remain.
Drain at cell exhaustion, end of available input, flush/close or exhausted
callback budget. Never wait to fill a batch. Flush is a barrier: drain all
preceding cells and the active snapshot, then resume that same request/state
with empty output storage. Compact any suffix once only after all borrows end.

A global64 callback budget, at most the effective batch limit per connection,
and rotating scan start bound dispatch work. Oldest-unsent deadlines remain;
checks surround application invocation, but a violating callback cannot be
preempted. A parser error or Connection: close response drains valid preceding
output. Handler `.close`, invalid output or timeout can discard earlier unsent
cells. `finish()` returning does not promise a completed send.

Completed counts and request-cycle maxima are recorded at whole-batch drain.
A successfully sent prefix of a subsequently canceled batch may be omitted.
These are conservative completion observations, not individual latency events.
Config.heapBytes includes exact requested framework allocations, cells and gather
metadata; requested worker stacks are separate. Kernel/libc/pthread/app memory,
allocator overhead and RSS remain outside that bound. Ordinary kernel socket
copies remain; this is not SEND_ZC or NIC zero-copy.

## Correctness evidence and limits

At b7ac355, macOS M3 Max arm64, macOS26.6.2 build25G83, exact Zig0.16.0:
Debug and ReleaseSafe each passed 14/14 build steps,52/52 unit executions,
26 generic,10 inline,11 gather and15 batch cases. Linux ReleaseSafe passed the
same52+62 cases. The 32-distinct-generated-response fixture reduced sends32→2
and compaction25,251→816bytes. Distinct borrowed POST bodies survived23-byte
submissions. Mixed routes, limits1/2/4/16, one-byte sends, order barriers,
128 empty flush resumptions and3,585-response fairness fixtures passed.
These are bounded witnesses, not starvation or latency guarantees.

Review found that the original 2MiB-body cancel fixture could drain earlier
responses before that body completed. It did not witness several frozen cells
at cancellation. Checkpoint5620905 therefore adds a separate depth16 pipeline
of complete requests for a startup-loaded65,535-byte asset, tiny socket buffers,
a1s server deadline and finite process/client watchdogs. Its counter observes
retained cells when pending gather cancellation is successfully requested;
a target may still race normal completion. Exact65536-byte input initially
failed StreamTooLong because Zig's readFileAlloc limit is exclusive; the final
fixture and documentation retain the65,535-byte boundary.

Mac ReleaseSafe's16-case batch suite witnessed16 retained cells,80 short send
completions, one pending cancel and one canceled target terminal, then zero
owners/late allocations. Linux's separate witness retained16 cells, observed two short send completions
and one pending cancellation request; the target completed normally in the race,
so its canceled-target counter was zero. Both target and cancel owners drained.
At5620905, both native hosts passed52 Debug and52 ReleaseSafe unit executions,
26 generic +10 inline +11 gather +16 batch cases and30,000 exact-body ReleaseSafe
smoke responses. Native packet files accompany this report. A cancellation acknowledgement alone never frees target storage.

## Next measured work

Read-only review identifies remaining code costs: full operation-array scans at
admission and completion, whole-slot scheduler scans, six monotonic samples per
ordinary inline request, and generic header formatting. These are not profiled
attributions. Next isolate token-addressed Linux data/cancel cells while retaining
exact token/generation/kind assertions and separate terminal ownership. Compare
configured capacity128 versus1024 with identical active clients, then evaluate
fixed startup I/O shards for multicore throughput. Per-request offload, dynamic
lease release, fault/schedule simulation, sustained combined-limit loads,
HTML/macOS contender comparisons and qualified request tails remain queued.

## Deeper client pipelines, unchanged server batch limit

The user requested depths above16. Checkpoint
**3f1963f21a8d5c84b08efed94c90e1cbb9434330** extends the maintained wrk harness
and wire tests to32/64/128 without changing Zig server source from5620905.
Linux ReleaseSafe binary SHA-256:
`43719cb64d0c26be956eddf79bd96d3dd521d41d51c0f8c6d71050b33f6aa53d`.
Mac and Linux passed all22 batch cases, including distinct generated output and
borrowed POST bodies at every new depth, repeated connection reuse, batch≤16,
callbacks≤64 and zero live owners/late allocations. Exact body/order fixtures
are separate from timed wrk validation.

The [24-trial depth sweep](2026-09-05-batch/deep-pipelines.json) ran
17:44:01–17:46:59 UTC. Both servers use CPU0; clients remain CPUs3–7/four threads,
128connections,3repetitions,1s warmup+5s measured, shuffled seed20260905. Each
trial verifies two full pipelines of exact bodies/headers at its selected depth.
Server response_batch_limit stays16 and all startup limits remain unchanged.

| Client depth | Zig median responses/s (range) | libreactor median (range) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 1,160,475 (1,146,088–1,171,266) | 2,695,065 (2,471,274–2,697,257) |
| 32 | 1,159,432 (1,153,145–1,172,363) | 4,371,778 (4,226,190–7,136,099) |
| 64 | 1,063,927 (1,014,559–1,144,693) | 5,939,668 (5,932,495–6,037,804) |
| 128 | 1,189,968 (1,006,929–1,206,939) | 7,412,593 (7,109,447–7,708,741) |

All trials/warmups passed:388,038,368 timed responses,2,880 exact preflight
responses, zero wrk transport/status errors. Zig retained batch≤16/callbacks≤64,
zero timeouts/refusals/late allocations and zero final owners. Deeper client
pipelines did not expand response storage. They did increase suffix compaction:
zero bytes at16, roughly174–178MB at32,458–525MB at64 and1.05–1.31GB at128 across
whole trial sessions. More copying is observed; this alone does not quantify its
share of the throughput plateau. Larger startup server batch limits, deferred
or segmented input, and scheduler/operation lookup changes need separate tests.

The repeated depth16 control is below the earlier1.83M result. Preserve both
sweeps and their source identities; do not cherry-pick the faster one as current
capacity. A following same-sweep old/current binary control checks whether that
change is explained by the added cancellation diagnostic versus run conditions.
No result from a deeper client pipeline is relabeled as TechEmpower's depth16
workload. The known wrk corrected-percentile limits apply throughout.


The [six-trial code control](2026-09-05-batch/code-control.json) passed with zero
reported errors. Under the same one-core mask/depth16, current binary samples
were1,806,564 /1,160,185 /1,016,938 responses/s; original batch samples were
964,131 /1,091,957 /1,156,666. Seeded shuffling happened to place all current
trials before all original trials, so time and binary remain confounded.
The unchanged current binary itself spans the earlier fast and slow regimes;
this does not establish a cancellation-counter regression or identify the
source of variation. The code change's cost remains unquantified. A controlled
host/frequency/migration investigation is required before tight capacity claims.
These failed attribution conditions are retained, not averaged away.
